name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,627

clue.text: See 14
Crowd surrounding soldiers in swampy region

indicators.note: to surround something is to enclose it, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: a mass is a large crowd of people
OR is Other Ranks, ordinary soldiers as opposed to officers

explanation.surface: A crowd forms around troops caught in a bog.
explanation.walkthrough: Other Ranks, the ordinary soldiers below officer level, is a standard crossword abbreviation; 'in' just links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A morass is a bog or marsh, literally an area of soft wet ground.

clue.text: Frenchman, one stopping gift, shows total control

indicators.note: to stop a gap is to plug it, so these letters sit inside the other word

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation of Monsieur, a French title
the Roman numeral for one
a donation is something given

explanation.surface: A Frenchman blocking a gift seems to be a power play.
explanation.walkthrough: M for Monsieur is the usual crossword Frenchman; here it travels with the one, both plugging the gift together.
explanation.definitionFit: Domination is complete power or mastery exercised over others, so it is a fair synonym.

clue.text: Sailor trapped in offensive likely to survive

indicators.note: something trapped is held inside, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: vile means disgusting or offensive
AB is an able seaman, a sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor caught up in a military offensive might still pull through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offensive' reads as a military attack, but it is the adjective VILE; AB is the standard crossword sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: Viable originally describes a foetus or seed capable of living and growing, hence able to survive.

clue.text: Make small dish to hold one tart without filling

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within, so these letters go inside
with its filling gone a word keeps only its outer letters, the crust

blocks.note: a dish is slang for an attractive woman, a belle
the Roman numeral for one
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A recipe step: use a little dish for a tart with no filling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dish' and 'tart' suggest cooking, but dish is a good-looking woman (BELLE) and the tart loses its filling to leave TT.
explanation.definitionFit: To belittle someone is to make them seem small or unimportant by disparaging them.

clue.text: Really enthusiastic, great female singer turned up

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning a word up means reading it from bottom to top

blocks.note: a diva is a celebrated female opera singer

explanation.surface: A fan raves that a great female singer showed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' reads as arrived, but in a down entry it means the word goes in upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Avid means keen or eager, describing someone with strong enthusiasm for an interest.

clue.text: See 27
China with crack not worth considering

blocks.note: china is cockney rhyming slang for mate (china plate), so a pal
to have a crack at something is to have a try

explanation.surface: Crockery with a crack in it is hardly worth keeping.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about cracked porcelain, but china is rhyming slang: china plate means mate, a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Paltry means trivial or meagre, too small or petty to deserve any serious attention.

clue.text: Brute concealing old record is to put things straight

indicators.note: to conceal something is to hide it within, so the other letters are held inside

blocks.note: an ape is a brutish creature
O is the standard abbreviation for old
a log is a written record, as of a voyage
taken as written

explanation.surface: A brute hiding an old criminal record now wants to make amends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' looks like the link to the definition, but it is held inside the brute with the old record; the real link is 'to'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying sorry is a way of making amends, settling a wrong and restoring good relations with someone.

clue.text: Football team in very unfortunate article

blocks.note: V is the abbreviation for very
ill as in ill luck means unfortunate
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A newspaper runs a damning piece about a football club.
explanation.walkthrough: Aston Villa is a Birmingham football club in England's Premier League, usually called just Villa.
explanation.definitionFit: Villa is the everyday short name for the Birmingham club Aston Villa, an English soccer side.

clue.text: Arab or Irish-American taking first question?

blocks.note: IR is an abbreviation for Irish
A is a standard abbreviation for American
first question is Q1, and the digit 1 reads as the letter I

explanation.surface: A quiz asks whether someone is Arab or Irish-American before the opening question.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen makes Irish-American look like one nationality, but it splits into IR and A; Q1 then supplies the last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Most people of Iraq are Arabs, so a native of that country can be described this way.

clue.text: Shades grass area where vision obscured

blocks.note: window blinds shade a room from light
grass and pot are both slang for cannabis

explanation.surface: Sunglasses and cannabis make a spot where you can't see clearly.
explanation.walkthrough: The S of the plural shades moves across the word break, so the cut between pieces falls one letter later than the enumeration.
explanation.definitionFit: A blind spot is a region of the visual field, or of a driver's view, that cannot be seen.

clue.text: Kidnapped person and entertainer get on

blocks.note: a host entertains guests
to get on is to grow older

explanation.surface: A captive and a showbiz performer seem to hit it off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get on' suggests getting along with each other, but it means growing old.
explanation.definitionFit: A hostage is someone seized and held captive until demands are met, as in a kidnapping.

clue.text: Women's magazine goes for Hitchcock film

blocks.note: a long-running British weekly magazine for women, its title a polite word for a woman with the definite article
to go is to disappear

explanation.surface: A women's magazine runs a feature on an Alfred Hitchcock movie.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lady is a British magazine aimed at women, founded in 1885; 'goes' supplies the verb that ends the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Hitchcock directed this 1938 British thriller about an elderly passenger missing from a train.

clue.text: Display attitude that's no longer relevant?

blocks.note: ex- means former, no longer current
a position is a stance or attitude on an issue

explanation.surface: Showing a stance that has gone out of date.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the word as ex-position, a former attitude; the question mark flags the playful split.
explanation.definitionFit: An exposition is a public exhibition or show, a display of goods or works.

clue.text: Posh sons in boat cut fare from Japan

indicators.note: a cut word is shortened, losing its final letter
letters placed in something go inside it

blocks.note: U means upper class, posh
S is the abbreviation for son
a ship is a boat; with its tail cut it loses its last letter

explanation.surface: Well-to-do boys on a boat trip eat Japanese food.
explanation.walkthrough: SHIP is cut to SHI, then U and S go inside after its S.
explanation.definitionFit: Sushi is a Japanese dish of vinegared rice with raw fish, so it is food from Japan.

clue.text: Very old and wise person circling pitch

indicators.note: to circle something is to go right round it, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: a sage is a wise person
pitch in music is the tone of a note

explanation.surface: An ancient wise man walks round a sports pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' suggests a playing field, but it is a musical sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Stone-age describes something extremely old-fashioned, as if from prehistoric times before metal tools.

clue.text: I felt that initially extravagant need to pay

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter counts

blocks.note: ow is what you say when something hurts
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone winces at an extravagant bill they must settle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I felt that' is a cry of pain, rendered as the exclamation OW.
explanation.definitionFit: To owe money is to be under an obligation to pay it back to someone.

clue.text: Silly to repeat work by Gilbert and Sullivan?

indicators.note: silly means foolish or nonsensical, so the letters are muddled up

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint that a Gilbert and Sullivan show is a foolish repeat.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a definition by example: the Savoy works are one kind of light opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Gilbert and Sullivan wrote comic light operas such as The Mikado, the classic examples of the genre.

clue.text: Saintly gatekeeper's famous rabbit

blocks.note: first meaning: the apostle who keeps the gates of heaven
second meaning: Beatrix Potter's mischievous rabbit

explanation.surface: The keeper of heaven's gate turns out to be a well-known rabbit.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is short for 'is', joining two separate characters who share a name.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Peter traditionally holds the keys of heaven, and Beatrix Potter wrote the tale of the rabbit with that name.

clue.text: Kept talking though disheartened and betrayed

indicators.note: losing heart means losing the centre, so the middle letter goes

blocks.note: to rattle on is to chatter at length

explanation.surface: Someone kept talking despite being downhearted and let down.
explanation.walkthrough: The nine-letter phrase has L at its centre; removing it leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To rat on someone is informal for informing against them, a betrayal of trust.

clue.text: Helpful creature shows way to get good marks

blocks.note: in folklore a small helpful household sprite that does chores at night
someone who indicates a direction with a finger shows the way

explanation.surface: A helpful little creature knows the way to win approval.
explanation.walkthrough: Brownies were house elves of Scottish and English folklore who did chores at night.
explanation.definitionFit: These are notional credit earned for good deeds, especially by currying favour with someone in charge.

clue.text: Smallest room with pictures showing film star

blocks.note: the smallest room is a euphemism for the toilet, bog in British slang
pictures are works of art

explanation.surface: A lavatory decorated with a poster of a movie star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The smallest room' is a British euphemism for the toilet, and bog is British slang for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Humphrey Bogart was the Hollywood actor of Casablanca, one of cinema's biggest names.

clue.text: Perfectionist's fine American pickle

blocks.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
US is short for the United States, so American
to be in a pickle is to be in a tight spot

explanation.surface: A perfectionist takes pride in a fine American relish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pickle' looks like food, but here it means a predicament.
explanation.definitionFit: A fusspot is someone overly particular about small details, much like a perfectionist.

clue.text: Presentation intended to reach Hancock shortly?

indicators.note: shortly means in brief, so the name is cut short by its last letter

blocks.note: a letter for someone is meant to reach them
Matt Hancock was a UK government minister; his first name loses a letter

explanation.surface: A presentation is meant to reach a famous Hancock soon.
explanation.walkthrough: Matt Hancock was the British Health Secretary during the pandemic; the question mark warns that only his first name, docked, is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Format is the way something is arranged or presented, such as the layout of a show or page.

clue.text: See 21
Substantial support for stars here?

definitions.note: a cryptic pointer to a constellation, not a noun phrase

blocks.note: great means large or substantial
to bear a load is to support it

explanation.surface: Asks where you might find strong backing for celebrities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' looks like celebrities, but means the stars in the night sky; the question mark admits the loose definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ursa Major is a large northern constellation, whose seven brightest members form the Plough or Big Dipper.

clue.text: Actor Herbert leaves home?

blocks.note: first meaning: the surname of Herbert Beerbohm, the Victorian actor-manager
second meaning: the place where foliage lives

explanation.surface: An actor named Herbert walks out on his family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb but is the plural noun; the question mark admits the whimsical definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbert Beerbohm Tree founded RADA, and foliage grows on the branches of a woody plant.

clue.text: One in dancing went to twist together

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and change places
letters placed in something go inside it

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone went dancing to do the Twist with a partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twist' hints at the dance, but it belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To twine strands is to wind or plait them around each other, twisting them into one.

clue.text: Trumpeter leaving band needs help with entourage assembled

indicators.note: to assemble is to put parts together in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A trumpet player who quit the group now needs support from hangers-on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trumpeter' and 'band' suggest a musician, but the trumpeting animal has left its herd.
explanation.definitionFit: An elephant trumpets, and a rogue one lives apart from its herd, often behaving aggressively.

clue.text: Devastate a fort wounding number inside!

indicators.note: the letters needed sit within the words before it, spanning their boundaries

blocks.note: a run of letters straddling the four words

explanation.surface: A battle cry: devastate the fort, wound those within!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' looks part of the battle scene but is the definition, a song; the letters run from the end of 'Devastate' into 'wounding'.
explanation.definitionFit: A number is a song in a show, and this is a well-known 1925 standard from No, No, Nanette.
